newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong Governor Patten to visit London.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong Governor Patten to visit London.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten is to visit London this month when he is expected to brief the incoming Labour government on the British colony ahead of its imminent handover to China.
Patten flies to London on May 17 and will likely spend several days in Britain, a Hong Kong government spokesman said on Sunday.
Patten's job as the 28th and last British governor of Hong Kong ends when the territory of 6.4 million people reverts to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.

Patten, a former Conservative party chairman credited with masterminding the party's 1992 general election victory, has kept out of the limelight since the party's crushing defeat ended 18 years in power in last week's elections.

Speculation is rife that he harbours ambitions to return to British politics although Patten insists he plans only to take six months off, potter around his garden and write a book about Europe and Asia.
He told Britain's Sky Television he had no plans to contest the Conservative party leadership.
Incoming Foreign Secretary Robin Cook has endorsed Patten and announced the new Labour government has no plans to change British policies on Hong Kong.

Derek Fatchett the man tipped to become the foreign office minister in charge of Hong Kong affairs said Britain would monitor events in the territory after the handover and was prepared to defend Hong Kong's freedoms.
"We would argue in defence of what has been signed by both the British and Chinese sides," the English-language Hong Kong Standard quoted Fatchett as saying from London.
"The essential democratic freedoms enjoyed by Hong Kong people are relevant to the economic success of Hong Kong and they must remain intact," he said.
Hong Kong is guaranteed a high degree of autonomy for 50 years under an agreement signed by China and Britain in 1984.
